scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the asshole)** **Here's why, legally and ethically:** ### ️ **You are enforcing a court-ordered schedule** - Your parenting time is ** legally binding**. The ex cannot unilaterally cancel or reschedule it for her convenience (e.g., "amusement park," "4th of July party") under the guise of " what's best for the son." Courts prioritize consistency and stability for children, and *your* scheduled time is part of that stability. - **"It's for the son" is a manipulation tactic** when used to override court orders. If the ex genuinely believed an activity was in the son's best interest (e.g., a medical emergency), she’d need to *discuss it with you first* and potentially seek a *formal modification* of the custody agreement through court—not just demand you give up your time. ### ️ **You’ve been accommodating *too* much** - You describe a pattern where you’ve "always tried to be accommodating" (e.g., giving up Wednesday overnight for a cousin visit, then being told "I need to stop being grumpy" when you asked for your son back). This has **normalized her behavior** and eroded your rights. - **Setting boundaries is healthy co-parenting**. By finally saying "no" to her last-minute changes during *your* time, you’re modeling respect for boundaries for your son. Kids thrive when both parents consistently enforce rules and schedules. ### ️ **The ex is the one acting unreasonably** - **She’s using the son as a shield** to avoid accountability. If she wanted the son to attend the amusement park or 4th of July party, she should have done so * during her own parenting time*— not during *yours*. - **Her " it’s for your son" excuse is a red flag**. Courts rarely side with a parent who repeatedly disrupts the other parent’s time for non-emergency personal activities (e.g., " family fun"). If this continues, you should: - **Document everything** ( texts, missed exchanges, pattern of changes). - **Consult a family lawyer** to formally address the violations (e.g., request make-up time, modify custody terms, or seek contempt of court if she’s flagrantly ignoring the order). ### 💡 **What you should do next** - **Keep your son during your scheduled time**. This is not " being difficult"— it’s upholding your legal rights. - **Reply to her firmly but calmly**: > * " I understand you have plans, but this is my court-ordered time. I will pick up [son] at [ agreed time] as scheduled. If you need to reschedule, we can discuss it through proper channels (e.g., a co-parenting app or lawyer), but I cannot give up my time for your personal activities."* - **If she refuses to comply**: - **Do not physically force the issue** (e.g., show up unannounced to " take" the son). - **Contact your lawyer immediately** to file a motion for enforcement. Courts take custody violations seriously, and this pattern could lead to penalties for her (e.g., fines, loss of custody time, or even modified custody arrangements in your favor). ### 🌟 **Final thought** You’re not the asshole—you’re a parent finally standing up for your rights and your son’s stability. **Consistency in co-parenting is what children need most**. By allowing her to repeatedly override your time, you’ve been *harming* your son’s sense of security. It’s time to prioritize * his* need for a reliable, structured relationship with both parents— starting with * your* time being respected. **You’re doing the right thing.** 💪
